primary_topics: Chapter 5 of 'A Centenary of Justice' -- CJP's speech at the 'Advocates' Forum for Media' (March 16, 2001, Linden Suites, Ortigas) explaining the Supreme Court's centenary policy on mediation as a remedy for clogged dockets and delayed justice

The case for Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR -- negotiation, conciliation, mediation, arbitration): litigation is tedious, expensive and often ends in 'broken relationships and permanent animosities,' whereas ADR methods are 'old methods with a new twist' that decongest dockets and produce more civilized, relationship-preserving solutions

Mediation's institutional anchoring: Rule 18 of the Rules of Court (pretrial), the Interim Rules on Corporate Rehabilitation, the E-Commerce Act and the Retail Trade Liberalization Law; the cautionary tale of Purefoods Corporation v. CA; and the Asia Foundation-funded PhilJA training under Boston-based mediator Annabelle T. Abaya

The cultural fit and the launch: mediation suits 'the Asian and Filipino ways of solving problems without loss of face' and is especially apt for continuing relationships; demonstrated during 'Settlement Week' (March 26-April 6) when 300 regional trial courts in Metro Manila, Cebu and Davao referred actual cases to 300 trained mediators
sub_topics: The docket problem: 'Filipinos are a litigious people'; the number of cases filed exceeds those decided, producing delayed justice; earlier solutions essayed in CJP's 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' (2000), one of which was to promote ADR, especially mediation

The civilizational frame: ancient disputes settled by 'superior muscles, swords or guns' -- 'Might dictated right'; gentility taught that 'right is better than might; the pen, more powerful than the sword; and reason, more reliable than aggression,' giving rise to constitutions, codes and courts

Litigation's disadvantages: tedious, time-consuming, stressful, expensive, and often ending in broken relationships and 'new cycles of violence'; the e-age trend is toward less confrontational, relationship-preserving alternatives

ADRs defined: negotiation, conciliation, mediation and arbitration -- 'by no means novel,' some older than litigation, but lately 'refined and polished'; 'old methods with a new twist' integral to the SC's judicial reform program

Institutional anchoring: Rule 18 of the Rules of Court requires trial courts to consider ADR at pretrial; the Interim Rules on Corporate Rehabilitation (Rule 4) make referral mandatory; the new Electronic Commerce Act and Retail Trade Liberalization Law encourage ADR use

Purefoods Corporation v. CA (June 19, 2000): the Court lamented that a 'simple case' over generators bought to ease the 1992 power crisis 'could have been resolved through mediation and conciliation' but was instead decided only in 2000, 'when the crisis was already over and the generators no longer needed'

Training infrastructure: an Asia Foundation grant funds SC and PhilJA workshops; Boston-based Filipino mediator Annabelle T. Abaya (graduate studies at the University of Massachusetts and Harvard) retained to direct the training of mediators and mediation advocates

Mediation's advantages and cultural fit: 'more than litigation or arbitration, it will bring solutions to disputes speedily, conveniently and peacefully'; less confrontational, conforming to 'the Asian and Filipino ways of solving problems without loss of face'; especially apt for continuing relationships (family, labor, tenancy in economic/freeport zones, commercial, consumer, barangay-level)

'Settlement Week' (March 26-April 6): over 300 regional trial courts in Metro Manila, Cebu and Davao simultaneously refer actual cases to 300 trained mediators to demonstrate that mediation 'can resolve conflicts speedily, conveniently and peacefully'

The appeal to media: CJP asks media to help PhilJA and the SC inform the public about 'this old method with a new Philja twist,' predicting mediation vocabulary will become as familiar as phrases the public learned during the Senate impeachment trial

stances.claim: Mediation is not merely a docket-decongesting expedient but a civilizationally superior mode of dispute resolution: where litigation often 'inflicts deeper wounds and engenders vengeance,' mediation 'ushers in better harmony and improved relationships in the future,' and it fits 'the Asian and Filipino ways of solving problems without loss of face' -- making it especially apt for continuing relationships.
stances.rhetorical_move: mediation-as-civilizational-advance: positioning ADR within the long arc from might-makes-right to reason, and as culturally congruent with Filipino face-saving, rather than as a mere efficiency tool
stances.confidence: asserted as the governing rationale for the SC's mediation policy

stances.claim: ADR methods are 'old methods with a new twist' -- some older than litigation itself -- now refined into an integral part of judicial reform; their proper and extensive use 'would not only decongest court dockets, but also result in better and more civilized solutions to human disputes.'
stances.rhetorical_move: old-method-new-twist framing: legitimizing the reform by rooting it in ancient practice while crediting the SC/PhilJA with its modern refinement

notable_anecdotes: The Purefoods generators: CJP cites Purefoods Corporation v. CA, where a dispute over generators bought to ease the 1992 power crisis dragged through full litigation and was decided only in 2000 -- 'when the crisis was already over and the generators no longer needed by the buyer' -- as a cautionary example of a 'simple case' that mediation could have resolved in its infancy.

Settlement Week at scale: to prove the concept, over 300 regional trial courts in Metro Manila, Cebu and Davao would simultaneously refer actual cases to 300 trained mediators during 'Settlement Week' (March 26-April 6), aiming to resolve conflicts 'from a few hours to a maximum of a few days.'

Mediation entering everyday speech: CJP predicts mediation vocabulary will become as familiar to the public as 'your Honor,' 'objection sustained' and 'irrelevant and immaterial' -- phrases people had recently learned watching the Senate impeachment trial.

The Harvard-trained mediator: the Court retained Boston-based Filipino mediator Annabelle T. Abaya, with graduate studies at the University of Massachusetts and Harvard, to direct the training of mediators -- her experience spanning 'small family problems to mind-boggling international disputes.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces CJP's speech at the 'Advocates' Forum for Media' (March 16, 2001, Linden Suites, Ortigas), explaining the Supreme Court's centenary push for mediation as a remedy for clogged dockets and delayed justice -- a problem he had earlier addressed in 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' (2000). He opens with a civilizational arc: ancient disputes were settled by 'superior muscles, swords or guns' where 'Might dictated right,' until gentility taught that 'right is better than might; the pen, more powerful than the sword; and reason, more reliable than aggression,' giving rise to constitutions, codes and courts. But litigation, he notes, is 'tedious, time-consuming, stressful, expensive,' and often ends in 'broken relationships and permanent animosities,' sometimes inflicting 'deeper wounds' and 'new cycles of violence.' The e-age alternative is Alternative Dispute Resolution (negotiation, conciliation, mediation and arbitration) -- 'old methods with a new twist,' some older than litigation, now refined into an integral part of judicial reform. He cites their institutional anchoring (Rule 18 of the Rules of Court at pretrial, the Interim Rules on Corporate Rehabilitation, the E-Commerce Act and the Retail Trade Liberalization Law) and the cautionary case of Purefoods Corporation v. CA, where a dispute over generators bought to ease the 1992 power crisis was decided only in 2000, 'when the crisis was already over.' Focusing on mediation, he describes Asia Foundation-funded PhilJA training directed by Boston- and Harvard-trained Filipino mediator Annabelle T. Abaya, and argues mediation's distinctive value: it resolves disputes 'speedily, conveniently and peacefully,' conforms to 'the Asian and Filipino ways of solving problems without loss of face,' and is especially apt for continuing relationships (family, labor, tenancy, commercial, consumer and barangay-level). He announces 'Settlement Week' (March 26-April 6), when over 300 regional trial courts in Metro Manila, Cebu and Davao would simultaneously refer actual cases to 300 trained mediators, and closes by asking media to help PhilJA and the Court popularize 'this old method with a new Philja twist.'
